Subject: Pathfinder connector evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Alice / Tom — thanks again for walking through Evergreen Bank's private deployment objectives this morning. As discussed, Evergreen's two primary constraints are: (1) strict principle of least privilege for data plane access and (2) a requirement for predictable latency for inference traffic (95th pct < 40ms within region).

I've put together a short evaluation plan so we can align on which connectivity option (VPC peering, PrivateLink / interface endpoints, or site-to-site VPN) best fits Evergreen's compliance and ops model. Key questions for Evergreen to confirm:
- Do you need per-tenant network isolation inside your VPCs, or is a shared-internal-VPC acceptable?
- Will the traffic originate from on-premise data centers or solely from Evergreen-managed VPCs?
- Any appliance or IDS/IPS in the path that would block mTLS or dynamic port ranges?

Attached: a compact comparison workbook with latency/cost/operational checklists. Proposed next step: 30-min call Wednesday to review tradeoffs and pick a primary + fallback path.

Thanks,
Mina Haddad
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Pathfinder connector evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Mina / Alice — quick notes from a network-ops perspective after glancing at the topology you shared: 
- If Evergreen's inference clients are primarily inside a single production VPC, VPC peering is the lowest-friction and lowest-latency option. No cross-account interface endpoints to manage, but it does require route tables and CIDR management.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) provides the cleanest security boundary (no route propagation between VPCs) and supports granular IAM + endpoint policies, which looks attractive for the bank's least-privilege requirement. Expect slightly higher egress cost and a small latency bump (~2–6ms) from the ENI.
- Site-to-site VPN is only appropriate if a large portion of traffic originates from on-prem. Performance is the least predictable; headroom depends on your VPN device and encryption offload. For predictable 95p latency <40ms, VPN is risky unless you use a dedicated MPLS/VPN circuit or an SD-WAN with measured SLAs.

I'll prepare a quick matrix of operational maintenance windows and failure modes for our call.
Tom

Thanks, Mina / Tom. A few clarifications from the Evergreen side: 
- Most inference calls will originate from app servers that are in two production VPCs (payments-prod and analytics-prod) across the same AWS account. We are not yet routing inference requests from on-prem servers except for a small DR site (~10% of traffic).
- Compliance team requires that customer data paths cannot be transitive across systems we don't explicitly authorize. We prefer solutions that make it obvious which flows exist (visibility/flow logs).
- We currently have an F5 in the payments path and a Palo Alto between our VPCs for east-west segmentation. Any solution that requires broad CIDR exposure across accounts will need an exemption.

Prefer to prioritize a solution that is easiest to audit and restrict by service identity.
Alice

Subject: Re: Pathfinder connector evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Alice — given your constraints (two prod VPCs in same account + auditability + perimeter appliances), my recommendation is: 
Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) into a dedicated Redwood ingress VPC. Rationale: 
- Least transitive exposure: endpoints are ENIs that can be tightly controlled with security groups and endpoint policies.
- Auditability: VPC Flow Logs + Endpoint policies give explicit logs of which service principals are allowed. Easier to show to compliance than route tables.
- Appliance compatibility: Because traffic terminates at the ENI you can still put the Palo Alto in front of the ENI (or use a service proxy in your VPC).

Fallback: VPC Peering between payments-prod and an Evergreen-managed ingress VPC only if you want slightly lower latency and are comfortable with route table rule discipline and explicit CIDR allocations per environment. Avoid peering across accounts unless absolutely necessary (cross-account peering makes auditing trickier).

Caveats: 
- PrivateLink adds per-hour endpoint and per-GB data processing costs. We'll quantify in the workbook.
- If DR traffic will be routed over VPN, we'll need a failover plan that preserves security group mappings and NAT behavior.

If you want, Connor and I can put together a short playbook (MOP) showing an endpoint deployment pattern that wires the F5 -> Palo Alto -> endpoint ENI flow.

—Kimberly

Adding an operational checklist and failure-mode notes: 
- Monitoring: ensure ENI-level metrics (bytes in/out per endpoint) and VPC Flow Logs to a central S3 + Athena prefix. Set alerts on sustained throughput that would drive cost or latency changes.
- IAM / Endpoint policies: use least-privilege service principals (per-app role) not CIDR whitelisting where possible.
- Failover behavior: document NACL and SNAT interaction; when falling back to VPN for DR, source IPs could change (if NAT applied) which may affect application auth. Test for header-based auth assumptions.
- Security testing: run a dry-run with a synthetic workload to validate 95p latency and packet loss under expected load.

I'll take point on the MOP and schedule a 1-hour runbook session with your NetOps team next week if that works.

Connor O'Brien
